cells.tense: What they do with what's in front of them has become shared work, and they are standing in it now.
cells.ask: When a match is real, bend one practice of yours toward it on purpose — one session aimed at the two of you instead of at you.
cells.core:
The practice and the thing you're practicing for have merged. You can feel when a match is real, and when it is, repeating gets easy — you put your way of doing something next to another's and single work comes out of it. You stop rehearsing and start tending. What you keep moving toward is starting to move back.

The ease doesn't hold by itself. A two-way thing asks for upkeep, and the upkeep is just that you keep noticing what happens when you meet — where the two of you are alike and where only one of you is flexible. When something shows up in how the two of you work, let that set your direction for the day. That's how the shared ground stays under you.
cells.sheetLine: You feel a real match, and you move toward it.
cells.verb: Deciding to move as one with what you take up — joining your way of doing something to another's until single work comes out of it.
cells.place: A place of one small light kept lit by hand — repetition only, no one watching, turning intention into skill that lives in the body.

cells.tense: If they keep bending their practice toward a fit they have not been given, the bending will crowd out the work itself.
cells.ask: Next time, run a whole session on your own practice with nobody else in mind — and leave unsettled whether it will ever be shared.
cells.core:
You're working as if the meeting has already happened. Every repetition is aimed at a fit that hasn't been handed to you yet — you rehearse the merge instead of doing the work that could lead to one, and steering toward something that isn't there costs more than the work itself. What grows is the strain, not the skill.

When this is working from the right place, you let the work sit for a while and things get room to come up on their own. So give up control of the timing. Keep at one practice and let it be worth doing whether or not it ever joins with anything. Get it strong enough to hold weight before you try to carry something else with it.

cells.tense: Somewhere behind them a practice went quiet and lonely, and they still stand at the edge of where it ended.
cells.ask: Pick one small practice you've done before and give it ten honest minutes today — no goal set for what it should produce.
cells.core:
The repetitions thinned and then stopped, and nothing is coming from what you carry. It isn't a partner that's gone — it's the returning. Your skill went quiet because you stopped turning it over, and standing in the doorway of something that once mattered is not the same as picking it up again.

You don't need a partner or a plan to make a new start. Small and steady is enough, an unfinished thing you come back to because it's yours. Sorting comes back before closeness does: knowing what's true to you again shows you where a real connection could ever be joined. Practice where your own eyes can find it, and let that be the whole of it for now.

cells.tense: They are already in the work — the pen has been down and the page is filling — without seeing whose hand holds it.
cells.ask: Show someone one practice you already run — no explaining, just do it in front of them once through.
cells.core:
You're already shaping what you do with your hands, and you describe it as something that joined on its own. The repetition is running — small choices you make, the way you return to one thing again and again — and nobody, including you, has said that's what you're doing. When something is aimed hard at a target, the aiming can carry you past a choice you were really making.

Go back to the simplest layer, the plain mechanical repetition with no one watching. Saying the practice out loud turns it from something that happens to you into something you keep. The quieter danger is very steady discipline with no person in it — it goes cold, and it starts serving only itself.
